title: Iron deficiency anaemia (adult)
subject: haematology-oncology
summary: Confirm iron deficiency with ferritin (below 15 micrograms/L diagnostic, below 45 suggestive, higher with inflammation), start once-daily or alternate-day oral iron, switch to IV iron if oral fails or is unsuitable, and always find the cause, including bidirectional endoscopy in men and postmenopausal women.

sections.title: Diagnose
items: Anaemia: Hb below 13 g/dL in men and below 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women. Confirm iron deficiency with iron studies before investigating the cause.
Serum ferritin is the single most useful test: below 15 micrograms/L is highly specific; below 30 generally indicates iron deficiency; AGA uses a cut-off of 45 ng/mL for better sensitivity.

Ferritin is an acute phase protein, so a normal value can hide iron deficiency during inflammation; ferritin above 150 micrograms/L makes absolute deficiency unlikely even with inflammation. Transferrin saturation below 20% supports iron restriction.
A rise in Hb of 1 g/dL or more within 2 weeks of oral iron supports the diagnosis.
Microcytosis with normal ferritin in India: consider beta thalassaemia trait (HbA2 above 3.5% on HPLC) and anaemia of inflammation; mixed iron with B12 or folate deficiency is common.

sections.title: Find the cause
items: History: diet (vegetarian), menstrual loss, pregnancies, blood donation, GI symptoms, NSAIDs or antithrombotics, previous gastric or bariatric surgery, family history of GI cancer or bleeding disorder.
All patients: urinalysis for haematuria and coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA).
Men and postmenopausal women with confirmed IDA: gastroscopy and colonoscopy as first-line investigations (CT colonography if unfit). Test for H. pylori non-invasively.
Premenopausal women: assess menstrual loss; endoscopy if GI symptoms, a strong family history of colorectal cancer, or IDA that persists or recurs despite treatment (AGA suggests a lower threshold).
Negative bidirectional endoscopy with poor response or recurrence: capsule endoscopy of the small bowel and renal tract imaging.
In endemic areas check stool for hookworm and other parasites.

sections.title: Oral iron
items: Start iron without waiting for investigations, unless colonoscopy is imminent.
One tablet a day of ferrous sulfate, fumarate or gluconate (50 to 100 mg elemental iron), ideally fasting; vitamin C may improve absorption. Do not give more than once daily.
If side effects occur: alternate-day dosing (similar absorption, better tolerated), a different formulation, or IV iron.
Check Hb at 2 to 4 weeks: expect a rise of at least 1 g/dL by 2 weeks, or 2 g/dL (or normal Hb) by 4 weeks. Failure predicts poor response and favours IV iron.
Continue for about 3 months after Hb normalises to replenish stores.

sections.title: IV iron and transfusion
items: Use IV iron if oral iron is not tolerated or ineffective, absorption is impaired (active IBD, coeliac disease, bariatric surgery), there is ongoing blood loss, rapid correction is needed, or in CKD and heart failure.

Prefer formulations that replace the deficit in 1 or 2 infusions. Ferric carboxymaltose: 20 mg/kg per infusion, maximum 1000 mg, over at least 15 minutes; repeat after 1 week if the deficit is larger.
Iron sucrose: 200 mg per dose by infusion over 30 minutes, up to 3 times a week, until the calculated deficit is given.
Total deficit (Ganzoni): weight (kg) x (target Hb minus actual Hb in g/dL) x 2.4, plus 500 mg for stores; a target Hb of 13 g/dL is often used.

Observe for 30 minutes after infusion. Most reactions are complement-mediated infusion reactions; true anaphylaxis is very rare. Do not give during bacteraemia. Ferric carboxymaltose often causes hypophosphataemia: check phosphate if repeated doses or risk factors.
Transfuse only for severe symptomatic anaemia or circulatory compromise (target Hb 7 to 9 g/dL), then complete iron replacement.

sections.title: India context and special groups
items: Anaemia Mukt Bharat (MoHFW) combines iron and folic acid supplementation, deworming, digital testing and treatment, and IV iron for moderate to severe anaemia in pregnancy; link patients to these services.
Deworm with albendazole 400 mg orally as a single dose where soil-transmitted helminths are common.
Pregnancy: follow the obstetric anaemia protocol; IV iron is used in the second and third trimesters, not the first.
CKD and heart failure: IV iron is usually preferred. After bariatric surgery: IV iron.

sections.title: Follow-up and non-response
items: Check FBC every 4 weeks until Hb is normal, then about 3-monthly for a year and 6-monthly for 2 to 3 years to detect recurrence.

Poor response: check adherence, continued bleeding, malabsorption (coeliac disease, H. pylori, atrophic gastritis), wrong diagnosis (thalassaemia trait, anaemia of inflammation), and B12 or folate deficiency.
Recurrent IDA with no reversible cause: long-term or intermittent iron replacement is reasonable.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating with iron but not looking for GI blood loss or cancer in men and postmenopausal women.
Twice or thrice daily iron: more side effects without better absorption (hepcidin rises after each dose).
Relying on a normal ferritin during inflammation, or missing thalassaemia trait.
Stopping iron as soon as Hb is normal.

drugs.name: Ferrous sulfate
drugs.dose: 200 mg tablet (65 mg elemental iron) orally once daily or on alternate days
drugs.notes: Continue about 3 months after Hb normalises.

drugs.name: Ferric carboxymaltose
drugs.dose: 20 mg/kg IV per infusion, maximum 1000 mg, over at least 15 minutes; may repeat after 7 days
drugs.notes: Monitor phosphate with repeated doses. Avoid in first trimester and during bacteraemia.

drugs.name: Iron sucrose
drugs.dose: 200 mg IV over 30 minutes per dose, up to 3 times a week, until the total deficit is replaced
